title: ☢️ Trump is radioactively unpopular
subtitle: Embracing Jensen Huang might hurt Huang more than it helps the president. Plus, listener questions on Still Counting EP14.
contentHtml:
Happy Thanksgiving Eve! I think we have a good little newsletter for you today, but let me link to this week’s Still Counting episode first:

Video above, audio below. In case you’re stuck on the tarmac somewhere, we tried to have some fun, talking about the Trump-backed restoration of Jensen Huang at Nvidia, the Democrats’ debate schedule, and answering several listener questions. And yes, our Thanksgiving wish is that you’ll comment, like, review and/or subscribe to the show.

The context

President Trump’s approval rating has steadily declined over the past two years. Believe me: we get some things wrong around these parts. We have before and we will again. But the idea that second terms hit different and have much lower approval floors was one of those points on which we were a little ahead of the curve.

On the podcast, we talked about how poorly Trump has performed as some kind of “populist”. I’m sorry if any of this comes across as partisan, but I’m trying to describe reality. In various ways, he’s betrayed his base.

The “Liberation Day” tariffs triggered an initial decline in Trump’s numbers, but at least they were broadly consistent with what he’d promised on the campaign trail. Going to war with Iran and spiking gas prices as a result wasn’t what he advertised, however. I don’t want to overindex on this, but talking a big game about releasing the Epstein files and then basically reneging wasn’t consistent with his promises either.

And then there’s this Nvidia story — and the broader embrace of Silicon Valley by the president and vice versa. Look, I respect Jensen Huang, and I don’t care who he slept with. Silicon Valley types almost seem to be promoting angles about his reported infidelity or his reported abusive treatment of staffers because it obscures the real issue here: that Nvidia’s best chips were reportedly winding up in the hands of China.

AI is the most important technology of my lifetime, and one of the most important in the history of the human species. It also plausibly follows winner-take-all dynamics, and it obviously has national security implications. I don’t think Huang’s position is incoherent. Maybe American leadership in the sector is so strong that we can afford to export Blackwell chips to China because we’re not going to forsake the lead. And maybe AI is a “normal technology,” as I think Huang and Nvidia honestly believe — although I don’t think they have much remaining credibility on the matter.

But Trump ran as a “China hawk.” Because I basically do think that AI is an extraordinary technology, and I’d put nuclear weapons in the same category, I’m going to make the obvious comparison here. What if Ronald Reagan had run as a USSR/Russia hawk, and yet also helped to facilitate the export of fissile material toward the Russians? I think he’d have been impeached and removed from office.

In making political forecasts, you’re often stuck between a rock and a hard place. Clearly we’re living in times of extremely high partisanship, and clearly also Trump retains a lot of influence on Republican legislators and executives. That caps his downside to some extent. But his ability to intimidate is severely negated after a completely embarrassing midterm result for the GOP. His party just lost a Senate seat in Missis-fucking-sippi. He’s never cared about anyone other than himself, and to the extent he worries about his popularity over the next two years at all, he seems to be unable to behave rationally. He’s 80 years old. I’m not even going to speculate about how and whether Trump Inc. is profiting off of chip sales to China, though there’s obviously room for responsible inferences on that question. (He does own a fair bit of Nvidia stock.)

But the American public isn’t tolerating this. Trump’s approval rating has declined to 35.9 percent as of today’s Silver Bulletin update. After Democrats considerably beat their polls on Nov. 3, in an election where the polls might have overestimated Republicans precisely because Trump is so unpopular that people didn’t want to admit to having voted for him, that ought to be a pretty solid figure.

What’s also been remarkable is the steadiness of Trump’s approval rating decline. There have been some bounces around events like Liberation Day, but you can do remarkably well with just a standard trendline1:

Trump approval rating vs. log-linear trendline

Don’t gas prices play a role? Well, yes, and lately they’ve been declining, thankfully. The uptick in gas prices after Labor Day probably contributed to the magnitude of the D landslide on Nov. 3. However, while gas prices on their own have been a good directional signal, they aren’t all that precise at replicating Trump’s approval rating. Recently, for instance, they would project improvement in his numbers when instead they’ve been getting worse:

Trump approval rating vs. gas-price trend

If you like, you can layer gas prices on top of the time trend. Although the trend is doing most of the work, they remain a statistically significant amplifier:

Trump approval rating vs. trendline + gas prices

I haven’t extended the trendlines past today, because this is meant to be descriptive, not predictive. To save you the time in case you were thinking about doing this yourself, though, extending the trendline outward would put Trump’s approval rating at around 27 percent by Election Day 2028, basically right where George W. Bush’s was at the end of his second term.

The latest downtick might be Nvidia or the (related) jitters in the stock market. Maybe some of it is also an artifact of pollsters being more confident in showing decrepit numbers for Trump after their midterm experience.

But I don’t want to lose the forest for the trees here. I think it’s notable how feeble attempts at intellectualizing Trumpism have been, but populism has a long tradition in American politics. Trump could semi-authentically claim to be a populist in 2016, and Hillary Clinton was a poor candidate, although she still won the popular vote. Democrats won the House popular vote by 8+ points in 2018, and then Trump became a seeming one-termer in 2020 in an election that was close in the key Electoral College states but a well-below-par performance for an incumbent.

Then Democrats fucked up in basically every possible way: through lax border policies, through excessive spending that triggered high inflation, and by trying to renominate a soon-to-be 82-year-old president who obviously wasn’t fit for the job. Wokeness and cultural trends and vibes may have played some part here too, though even as an unapologetically woke-agnostic pundit, I think it was probably in more of a “best supporting actor” role.

I think Trump has a certain amount of political acumen, but it’s probably also overrated. Hillary Clinton (who won the popular vote), 77-year-old Joe Biden (whom Trump lost to anyway), and Kamala Harris (after an obviously unfit-for-four-more-years president was forced out) are not exactly a murderers’ row of opponents. Maybe if Democrats had nominated Biden in 2016 — or who knows, maybe Bernie Sanders — he’d have been more of a historical footnote.

It’s easy enough to understand what Huang and Nvidia get out of this, although I don’t love the idea of possibly the most strategically important corporation in the world owing a favor to a profoundly corrupt president.

Silver Bulletin news and notes

Please do read Tuesday’s post on the AI x political moment if you haven’t yet. We try to make every newsletter worth your time, but I think that one was important.

Ironically, the AI tools are also helping us to build all kinds of cool interactives and features. So expect various things to land over the next 4-8 weeks.

Otherwise, I want to keep your expectations modest. Mid-November through early January is the closest thing we have to a slow period, and it’s a good time for long-term projects and for personal travel. Expect 2.5-ish posts per week, and then we’ll strive to increase that volume in the new year. We hope you’ll enjoy your Thanksgiving and beyond.

Oh, and we’re hiring. I’ll send out a few more reminders before the deadline closes in a few weeks.

Silver Bulletin is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider subscribing.

1

More specifically, a trendline based on a combination of a log and linear fit, but the linear fit alone would do almost as well outside of a honeymoon period when Trump first re-took office.
